title: The Atlas has no criteria for deciding when two Atlas Edit Proposals are in conflict
content:
The Needed Research track NR-18 opens with the question the Reconciliation Process assumes is already answered: "What criteria should be used to determine when two or more Atlas Edit Proposals are in conflict? Are conflicts strictly based on overlapping content, or do broader thematic or operational conflicts also count?"

This is a genuine gap rather than a drafting nicety. A.1.11.2.5.2 and A.1.12.2.7.2 build their entire branch structure on the distinction between "non-conflicting / logically compatible" edits, which the Core Facilitator may merge unilaterally, and "conflicting / logically incompatible" edits, which must be returned to voters. Neither Section defines the terms, so the trigger for the most consequential choice in the process — Facilitator discretion or a fresh vote — rests on an undefined predicate.

NR-18 names the hard case: "if two AEPs amend different sections of the Atlas but have implications that could lead to contradictory outcomes, how should the Core Facilitator identify and address this indirect conflict?" Textual overlap is detectable mechanically; semantic incompatibility across separate documents is not, and the Reconciliation Process is scoped explicitly to "the specific components that are being simultaneously edited" — which would miss it entirely.

A second open case is asymmetric scope: "What if one AEP effects a significant overhaul of an Atlas document, while another effects minor tweaks to the same component? How do the Facilitators determine which elements of which AEP should take precedence?" Here the edits genuinely collide, but treating them as symmetric alternatives misdescribes the situation — one is a rewrite and the other a patch.

The practical consequence today is that conflict detection is a judgment call by the same actor who benefits from finding no conflict, since a finding of compatibility lets them merge rather than convene another poll.
description: NR-18 leaves open whether conflict means overlapping content only, or extends to proposals amending different sections whose combined implications are contradictory.
